variables.meaning: the power of the eye, the combined power of its cornea and lens, which it adjusts to keep the image on the retina
the object distance, the distance from the eye to the object it is viewing
the image distance, which for clear vision must equal the lens-to-retina distance
the height of the object
the height of the image on the retina, negative because the image is inverted
the magnification of the image on the retina
the power of a spectacle or contact lens, negative for a diverging lens and positive for a converging one
the object distance, measured from the spectacle lens
the image distance, measured from the spectacle lens, negative for the virtual image the eye then views
the overall magnification of the microscope, the product of the magnifications of its elements
the magnification of the objective lens
the magnification of the eyepiece
the focal length of the objective lens
the focal length of the eyepiece
the object distance for the objective lens
the image distance for the objective lens, where the first image forms
the object distance for the eyepiece, the distance of the first image from it
the image distance for the eyepiece, where the final image forms
the numerical aperture of an objective, a measure of its light-gathering ability
the refractive index of the medium between the lens and the specimen
the angle of acceptance, the angle of the widest cone of rays the lens accepts from the specimen
half the angle of acceptance
the focal length of a camera lens
the diameter of the aperture controlling the light into the lens
the focal length of the objective, where the first image of a distant object forms
the focal length of the eyepiece
the object distance for the objective, essentially infinite for a telescope
the image distance for the objective, equal to its focal length for a distant object
the angular magnification, the ratio of the angle the image subtends to the angle the object subtends
the angle subtended by the object as viewed by the unaided eye
the angle subtended by the image the telescope forms
the wavelength of the light passing through the lens
the focal length of the lens for light of one wavelength
the angle the incoming light makes with the optical axis
the diameter of the aperture that admits light to the lens
the radius of curvature of the telescope mirror, twice its focal length

glossary.definition: the ability of the eye to adjust its focal length is known as accommodation
a condition in which the lens of the eye becomes progressively unable to focus on objects close to the viewer
another term for myopia, a visual defect in which distant objects appear blurred because their images are focused in front of the retina rather than being focused on the retina
a visual defect in which distant objects appear blurred because their images are focused in front of the retina rather than being focused on the retina
the object point imaged by the eye onto the retina in an unaccommodated eye
another term for hyperopia, the condition of an eye where incoming rays of light reach the retina before they converge into a focused image
the condition of an eye where incoming rays of light reach the retina before they converge into a focused image
the point nearest the eye at which an object is accurately focused on the retina at full accommodation
the result of an inability of the cornea to properly focus an image onto the retina
a medical procedure used to correct astigmatism and eyesight deficiencies such as myopia and hyperopia
identity of a color as it relates specifically to the spectrum
two types of photoreceptors in the human retina; rods are responsible for vision at low light levels, while cones are active at higher light levels
a theory that states that there are three primary colors, which correspond to the three types of cones
a part of the visual perception system that allows people to perceive color in a variety of conditions and to see some consistency in the color

a theory proposed to explain color and brightness perception and constancies; is a combination of the words retina and cortex, which are the two areas responsible for the processing of visual information
the ability to perceive color in an ambient-colored environment
a microscope constructed from two convex lenses, the first serving as the ocular lens(close to the eye) and the second serving as the objective lens
the lens nearest to the object being examined
the lens or combination of lenses in an optical instrument nearest to the eye of the observer

a number or measure that expresses the ability of a lens to resolve fine detail in an object being observed. Derived by mathematical formula $\text{NA} = n \sin \alpha$, where $n$ is the refractive index of the medium between the lens and the specimen and $\alpha = \theta/2$
optical technology in which computers adjust the lenses and mirrors in a device to correct for image distortions
a ratio related to the focal lengths of the objective and eyepiece and given as $M = -\frac{f_{\text{o}}}{f_{\text{e}}}$
failure of rays to converge at one focus because of limitations or defects in a lens or mirror
